difficultyReason: Three compound antecedent conditions, an 'unless' exception whose own antecedent must be checked, and a proportionality clause. Correct answer must satisfy all three conditions, show the exception does not trigger, and confirm the punishment scales with the harm. Traps satisfy the main conditions but fall under the exception, invert the proportionality requirement, or rely on a different subsidiary principle.
stimulus: A judge should impose the maximum statutory sentence on a convicted defendant only if (a) the crime caused serious and lasting harm to an identifiable victim, (b) the defendant planned the crime in advance rather than acting on impulse, and (c) the defendant has refused to acknowledge responsibility during the proceedings, unless the defendant suffers from a documented condition that substantially impaired deliberative capacity at the time of the offense. In every case, the severity of the sentence must be calibrated to the gravity of the harm inflicted.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delaney embezzled pension funds from retirees over three years, leaving several elderly victims unable to afford medical care. He planned each transfer carefully, has denied wrongdoing throughout trial, and has no documented cognitive impairment. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halvor set fire to an occupied warehouse, permanently injuring two employees, and methodically prepared the arson for weeks. Although he refused to apologize, a neurologist testified that a recently diagnosed frontal-lobe tumor had materially impaired his capacity for deliberation when he set the fire. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irendi defrauded a bank of a modest sum through an impulsive forgery. The bank reported no lasting harm, Irendi pled guilty on the first day, and no impairment was alleged. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence because deterrence requires a harsh signal to future offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jessan assaulted a stranger on the street, causing serious and lasting injury. The assault was unplanned, but Jessan has refused to acknowledge responsibility and is medically unimpaired. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Korath orchestrated a multi-year investment fraud that ruined several identifiable families. He denies responsibility and no impairment has been documented. The judge imposes the lightest sentence on the statutory scale, reasoning that financial crimes warrant leniency regardless of harm.

explanations.correct: Delaney's case satisfies every antecedent condition: serious and lasting harm to identifiable victims (retirees deprived of medical care), advance planning, and refusal to acknowledge responsibility. The exception does not trigger because Delaney has no documented impairment. The maximum sentence is described as matching the gravity of the harm, meeting the proportionality clause. The principle therefore prescribes the stated judgment.
explanations.B: Satisfies conditions (a), (b), and (c), but the documented frontal-lobe impairment triggers the exception. The principle withholds the maximum sentence whenever the exception's antecedent obtains, so the judgment contradicts the principle.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a) — no lasting harm — and condition (b) — the forgery was impulsive. The judge also invokes a deterrence rationale the principle does not recognize.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). Jessan's assault was unplanned, so the 'planned the crime in advance' requirement is unmet, regardless of how the other conditions fare.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Even where all antecedent conditions hold, the principle requires the sentence to be calibrated to the gravity of the harm; imposing the lightest sentence on a case of ruinous harm inverts that requirement.

difficultyReason: Three compound conditions plus an 'unless' exception governed by its own antecedent, plus a proportionality requirement tying intervention to demonstrated risk. Traps satisfy the main rule while falling under the exception or substitute a different justifying principle.
stimulus: A physician is justified in overriding a competent patient's refusal of treatment only if (a) the refusal would result in imminent and irreversible harm, (b) the patient's refusal rests on a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and (c) no less intrusive alternative is available, unless the patient has previously executed a valid advance directive refusing the specific intervention under the present circumstances. The degree of intervention imposed must be no greater than what is needed to prevent the imminent harm.
questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most closely conforms to which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Querin's patient refuses a ventilator, citing a correctly understood prognosis. The patient had previously signed a valid advance directive refusing ventilation under precisely these circumstances. Dr. Querin nonetheless intubates, reasoning that life preservation outweighs prior instructions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Palen's patient faces imminent organ failure and refuses dialysis on religious grounds. The refusal involves no factual misunderstanding, and Dr. Palen proceeds anyway because the harm is severe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Onwu's patient, bleeding internally, refuses a transfusion based on a mistaken belief that donated blood is routinely unscreened for pathogens. Dr. Onwu has provided documentation correcting the error, but the patient persists. No less intrusive alternative exists, and the patient has signed no advance directive. Dr. Onwu administers only the transfusion volume necessary to stabilize the patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Reymo's patient refuses antibiotics for a minor, non-life-threatening infection based on a misunderstanding about side effects. Dr. Reymo administers them covertly to spare the patient further argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Sendo's patient, facing imminent harm from sepsis, refuses a narrow-spectrum antibiotic due to a factual misunderstanding that Dr. Sendo has repeatedly tried to correct. No less intrusive option exists and no advance directive applies. Dr. Sendo administers a full course of broad-spectrum intravenous therapy exceeding what is needed to control the infection.

explanations.correct: Dr. Onwu's case satisfies every antecedent condition: imminent and irreversible harm (internal bleeding), a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and no less intrusive alternative. The exception does not trigger because no advance directive exists. The intervention administered is limited to what is needed to stabilize the patient, satisfying the proportionality requirement. The principle therefore justifies the override.
explanations.A: Triggers the exception. The patient executed a valid advance directive refusing the specific intervention under these exact circumstances, so the principle forbids override. The physician also substitutes a different subsidiary principle (life preservation) that the principle itself does not recognize.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). The refusal rests on religious grounds, not on a factual misunderstanding. The principle does not authorize overriding the refusal, even though the harm is severe.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — the infection is minor and not imminent — and condition (c) insofar as less intrusive alternatives (persuasion, delay, second opinion) plausibly exist.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality requirement. Although all antecedent conditions are met and no exception triggers, the principle caps intervention at what is needed to prevent the imminent harm; broad-spectrum therapy beyond that ceiling exceeds the licensed degree of intervention.

difficultyReason: Principle bundles three antecedent conditions, an exception whose antecedent itself must be verified, and a proportionality requirement. Distractors misfire at each branch: exception triggered, condition unmet, or disproportionate response.
stimulus: A regulator is warranted in imposing emergency restrictions on a newly discovered pollutant only if (a) credible evidence shows the pollutant poses a substantial risk of serious harm to public health, (b) the sources of the pollutant can be identified with reasonable confidence, and (c) ordinary rulemaking cannot deliver relief before the harm is likely to materialize, unless the pollutant is already adequately controlled by an existing regulation whose enforcement remains feasible. The scope of any restriction must be no broader than is needed to address the documented risk.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An agency imposes an emergency rule barring a newly characterized industrial solvent from use near residential zones after peer-reviewed studies link it to serious respiratory harm. The solvent's sources are limited to three identified facilities, ordinary rulemaking would take two years, no existing regulation covers the compound, and the rule's scope is confined to the residential-zone exposures that the studies document.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An agency imposes nationwide emergency restrictions on a solvent that has been linked in preliminary reports to mild skin irritation at high exposures. Sources are identified, rulemaking is slow, and no existing regulation covers the compound. The restriction applies to every use regardless of exposure level.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An agency imposes emergency restrictions on a compound credibly shown to cause serious harm. Sources are identified, rulemaking is slow, and the agency acts even though the compound is already adequately controlled by enforceable permit limits under a longstanding statute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An agency imposes emergency restrictions on a pollutant credibly shown to cause serious harm. Ordinary rulemaking would be too slow and no existing regulation covers the compound. The pollutant's sources, however, cannot be identified with any confidence; the agency acts on the basis of ambient monitoring alone.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An agency declines to impose emergency restrictions on a credibly dangerous, unregulated pollutant with identifiable sources and slow ordinary rulemaking, reasoning that emergency action is disfavored whenever industry cooperation seems possible.

explanations.correct: The agency's action satisfies every antecedent condition — credible evidence of serious harm, identifiable sources, and ordinary rulemaking too slow — and no existing adequate regulation triggers the exception. The scope is confined to the exposures documented by the underlying studies, meeting the proportionality clause. The principle licenses the restriction.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a): preliminary reports of mild irritation do not credibly show substantial risk of serious harm. The sweeping scope also violates the proportionality clause, which requires the restriction to be no broader than the documented risk.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The compound is already adequately controlled by an existing, enforceable regulation, so the principle withholds emergency authority even though the other conditions are met.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). Sources cannot be identified with reasonable confidence, so the principle does not authorize an emergency restriction.
explanations.E: Relies on a different subsidiary principle (favoring voluntary industry cooperation) that the principle stated above does not recognize. The stated conditions are satisfied, so the principle actually warrants action.

difficultyReason: The principle chains three conditions, an exception keyed to the employee's own prior conduct, and a proportionality clause tying remedy to demonstrated loss. Distractors either meet the main rule but trigger the exception, fail one condition, or impose a remedy out of proportion with the loss.
stimulus: An employer is entitled to recover training costs from a departing employee only if (a) the training was specialized and non-transferable, (b) the employee signed a written agreement acknowledging the recovery obligation before the training began, and (c) the employee departed voluntarily within the covenant's time window, unless the employee can show that the employer materially breached the employment contract before the departure. The amount recovered must not exceed the unamortized portion of the documented training cost.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firm W trained Pali in a specialized protocol, had her sign the recovery agreement before training, and she resigned within the covenant. Pali has documented that the firm stopped paying her earned commissions for four months before her departure — a material breach. The firm nonetheless recovers the unamortized cost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Firm Y trained Noor in a proprietary protocol and had her sign the recovery agreement afterward. Noor resigned voluntarily within the covenant period. The firm recovers the full training cost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Firm Z trained Oba in general office software. Oba signed the recovery agreement before training and resigned six months later, still within the covenant. The firm recovers the unamortized cost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Firm X trained Miko in a proprietary turbine-calibration protocol at a documented cost of $40,000. Miko signed the recovery agreement before training. She resigned nine months later to join a competitor, well within the two-year covenant. Firm X had not breached her contract. The firm recovers the $32,000 unamortized portion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Firm V trained Quen in a specialized, non-transferable process at a documented cost of $20,000. Quen signed the recovery agreement before training and resigned within the covenant. The firm had not breached her contract. The firm recovers triple the unamortized amount as a deterrent.

explanations.correct: Miko's case satisfies every antecedent condition: specialized, non-transferable training; a written agreement signed before training began; voluntary departure within the covenant. No material breach by the firm triggers the exception. Recovery is capped at the unamortized portion of the documented cost, satisfying the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Triggers the exception. The employer materially breached the employment contract by withholding earned commissions, so the principle denies recovery even though the other conditions are met.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). The recovery agreement must have been signed before the training began, not afterward. The timing requirement is not merely formal; it is part of the principle's antecedent.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a). General office software is not specialized, non-transferable training. The principle does not authorize recovery.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Even with every condition satisfied, recovery may not exceed the unamortized portion of the documented cost; tripling the amount for deterrence exceeds the principle's ceiling.

difficultyReason: Three stacked antecedent conditions, an exception whose antecedent is itself conditional on the researcher's past conduct, and a proportionality requirement on publication scope. Traps ignore the exception's antecedent, substitute a competing norm, or overreach the scope limit.
stimulus: A researcher is obligated to publish the negative results of a clinical trial only if (a) the trial was adequately powered to detect the effect being tested, (b) the protocol was preregistered in a public registry before enrollment began, and (c) the results bear directly on a treatment currently in clinical use, unless publication would reveal individually identifying patient information that cannot be redacted without rendering the data scientifically meaningless. The scope of any publication must be limited to the preregistered outcomes.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Ansari conducted a trial of a widely prescribed antihypertensive drug. The protocol was preregistered only after enrollment had concluded, even though the trial was adequately powered and the treatment remains in active clinical use. Patient identifiers can be redacted without loss of scientific meaning. Dr. Ansari publishes the preregistered outcomes, which are negative.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Belov ran an underpowered pilot study of a rarely used diagnostic reagent. Preregistration was completed, and the reagent is still in occasional use. Dr. Belov publishes the negative results to alert the field.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Carano conducted an adequately powered trial of a drug still in clinical use. The protocol was preregistered and no privacy concerns arise. Dr. Carano publishes a manuscript that includes the preregistered outcomes and adds an expansive post-hoc subgroup analysis that was not preregistered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Denu conducted an adequately powered, preregistered trial of a treatment still in clinical use. However, the trial recruited from a rural clinic so small that any redaction sufficient to protect patient identities would remove the data points needed to interpret the effect. Dr. Denu withholds publication.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Evora conducted a well-powered, preregistered trial of a drug already withdrawn from clinical use worldwide. No privacy risks arise. Dr. Evora publishes the negative results, reasoning that any negative result must be made public.

explanations.correct: Dr. Denu satisfies every antecedent condition — adequate power, preregistration, and direct bearing on a treatment in clinical use — but the exception's antecedent is also satisfied: redaction sufficient to protect identifying patient information would render the data scientifically meaningless. The exception's antecedent triggers, so the obligation to publish does not attach. Withholding publication conforms to the principle.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b). The protocol was preregistered only after enrollment concluded, not before it began. Preregistration timing is part of the principle's antecedent, so the obligation does not attach even though the other facts are favorable.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a) — the trial was underpowered — so the obligation does not attach. The researcher's choice to publish is permissible but not obligated by the principle.
explanations.C: Violates the proportionality clause. The publication's scope exceeds the preregistered outcomes by including a wide-ranging post-hoc analysis that was not preregistered.
explanations.D: Correct. The exception's antecedent is triggered.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). The drug is no longer in clinical use anywhere, so the results do not bear on a current treatment. The substituted principle ('any negative result must be made public') is not the principle stated.

difficultyReason: Three conjunctive conditions, an exception tied to the beneficiary's own prior conduct, and a proportionality clause. Distractors variously trigger the exception, fail a condition, substitute a different principle, or disregard proportionality.
stimulus: A municipality is justified in using eminent domain to take private property for a transit project only if (a) the taking is necessary to complete a transit corridor already adopted through public hearings, (b) feasible alternative routings have been studied and rejected on documented grounds, and (c) the owner has been offered compensation reflecting independent fair-market appraisal, unless the owner has been notified of the project for more than a decade and has made no material improvements during that period in reliance on the project's continuation. The compensation paid must be proportionate to the appraised loss and relocation costs.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Riverton takes a parcel owned by Hakim to complete the Green Line corridor adopted through three public hearings. Alternative alignments were studied and rejected on documented cost and grade grounds. Hakim is offered compensation based on an independent appraisal plus relocation costs. He has owned the parcel for four years and has invested heavily in a new workshop there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kestrel City takes a parcel for a proposed transit corridor that has been discussed but not formally adopted. Alternatives were informally ruled out in a closed meeting, and compensation offered matches the municipal assessor's internal estimate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Valborg takes a parcel owned by Senna to complete a corridor adopted through public hearings. Alternatives were studied and rejected on documented grounds. The city offers compensation based on a salaried staff assessor's in-house estimate rather than any independent appraisal. Senna has owned the parcel for four years and recently built a workshop on it. Senna sues; the court upholds the taking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marmont takes a parcel to complete an adopted corridor, studied alternatives and documented their rejection, but offers the owner no compensation, reasoning that public interest outweighs private compensation in transit cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Osune takes a parcel to complete an adopted corridor, studied and rejected alternatives, and pays the owner ten times the appraised value plus punitive damages to discourage future challenges, even though the owner's actual loss matches the appraisal.

explanations.correct: Riverton's taking satisfies every antecedent condition: the corridor was adopted through public hearings, alternatives were studied and documented as rejected, and Hakim received compensation based on independent fair-market appraisal. The exception does not trigger because Hakim has owned the parcel for only four years and has materially improved it. Compensation tracks the appraised loss and relocation costs, meeting the proportionality clause.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a) — the corridor was not formally adopted through public hearings — and condition (c), because compensation rests on an internal assessor's estimate rather than an independent appraisal.
explanations.C: Fails condition (c). Compensation based on a salaried staff assessor's in-house estimate is not compensation reflecting independent fair-market appraisal. The exception does not apply either, since Senna has owned the parcel only four years and has materially improved it. The principle does not justify the taking.
explanations.D: Fails condition (c). Refusing compensation substitutes a different principle (public-interest supremacy) that the principle stated does not recognize.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Compensation vastly exceeding appraised loss and relocation costs is not proportionate, regardless of the municipality's deterrent motives.

difficultyReason: Three conjunctive conditions, a narrow exception whose own antecedent turns on the broker's past conduct, and a proportionality clause limiting disgorgement to actual gains. Correct choice threads all three and confirms the exception is inactive.
stimulus: A securities broker has an obligation to disgorge profits from a trade only if (a) the trade was executed using material nonpublic information, (b) the information was obtained in the course of the broker's professional duties, and (c) the broker knew, or reasonably should have known, that the information was confidential when the trade was placed, unless the broker had, before learning the information, entered into a binding pre-committed trading plan that determined the trade's timing and size independent of any subsequent knowledge. The amount disgorged must not exceed the profits actually attributable to the trade.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broker Urbin heard a rumor at a public industry mixer that a small pharmaceutical firm would release disappointing trial data. He invested accordingly and earned substantial profits. He disgorges those profits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broker Tamsin learned from a client's earnings call preparation that the client would miss estimates. She knew this information was confidential, was acting in her professional capacity when she learned it, had no pre-committed trading plan, and personally sold the client's stock short, earning $60,000. She disgorges the $60,000.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Broker Vale obtained material nonpublic information while advising a client and traded on it, but her trades conformed precisely to a written trading plan she had preregistered with her compliance department nine months earlier, before she could possibly have learned the information. She disgorges her profits anyway to avoid regulatory scrutiny.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Broker Wren learned confidential merger information in the course of her duties and traded on it, earning $15,000. Regulators order her to disgorge $150,000 to serve as a strong deterrent to other brokers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Broker Xanh learned, in a casual conversation at a family dinner, confidential information about a firm she had no professional relationship with. She traded and earned profits. She disgorges her profits.

explanations.correct: Tamsin's case satisfies each antecedent condition: the trade used material nonpublic information, the information was obtained in the course of her duties, and she knew it was confidential. No pre-committed trading plan triggers the exception. Disgorgement is limited to the $60,000 actually earned, matching the proportionality clause. The principle prescribes the stated judgment.
explanations.A: Fails condition (a). Information overheard at a public industry mixer is not material nonpublic information obtained in a professional capacity; the principle does not authorize disgorgement on these facts.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The pre-committed trading plan was binding, predated the information, and determined the trades' timing and size independent of the later knowledge. The principle withholds the obligation to disgorge.
explanations.D: Violates the proportionality clause. Even though every condition is met, disgorgement may not exceed profits actually attributable to the trade; a $150,000 figure on $15,000 of gains exceeds the cap.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b). The information was not obtained in the course of the broker's professional duties. The principle does not reach the transaction regardless of the other conditions.

difficultyReason: Three compound conditions, an exception keyed to the speaker's prior role, and a proportionality requirement pegging response to actual disruption. Traps satisfy the main rule but trigger the exception, fail a condition, or overreach the proportional response.
stimulus: A university is justified in disciplining a student for disruptive speech at a campus event only if (a) the speech was made during a formally scheduled event at which attendance was open to the university community, (b) the speech prevented the scheduled speaker from being heard by the audience, and (c) the student had received a prior warning from a university official at the event, unless the student was a duly scheduled participant on the program whose allotted time had not yet concluded. Any disciplinary sanction imposed must be proportionate to the degree of disruption caused.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At a scheduled lecture open to the university community, Ida shouted over the invited speaker until the speaker abandoned the podium. A dean at the event had warned Ida in writing thirty minutes earlier to desist. Ida was not on the program. The university issues a one-semester probation, a sanction described as matched to the total loss of the lecture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At a scheduled public debate, Jari, the affirmative debater, spoke forcefully during his allotted fifteen minutes, overlapping occasionally with his opponent's reactions. The university expels Jari for disruption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In a private dormitory common room, Kem argued loudly with a visiting speaker until the speaker left. No university warning was issued and the gathering was not a formally scheduled event. The university suspends Kem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At a formally scheduled lecture, Lira heckled sporadically but the speaker continued and finished the lecture on schedule. Lira had been warned twice. The university expels Lira permanently.

choices.label: E
choices.text: At a formally scheduled lecture, Moir shouted over the speaker until the speaker abandoned the podium. No university official was present to warn Moir, but security escorted him out. The university issues a sanction matched to the degree of disruption.

explanations.correct: Ida's case satisfies every antecedent condition: a formally scheduled event open to the community, speech that prevented the speaker from being heard, and a prior warning from a university official at the event. The exception does not trigger because Ida was not a scheduled participant. A one-semester probation proportionate to the loss of the lecture meets the proportionality clause.
explanations.B: Triggers the exception. Jari was a duly scheduled participant speaking within his allotted time; the principle withholds discipline even if his speech overlapped with the opposing debater.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a) — the gathering was not a formally scheduled event — and condition (c), since no university warning was issued.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). The speech did not prevent the speaker from being heard. Expulsion also violates the proportionality clause, since the lecture concluded as scheduled.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). No warning from a university official was given at the event. Security action is not a substitute for the warning the principle requires.

difficultyReason: Three compound conditions, an exception whose own antecedent requires checking the vendor's disclosures, and a proportionality requirement on the remedy. Traps substitute a competing principle, fail a condition, or overreach the cap.
stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund from a vendor only if (a) the product materially failed to perform as described in the vendor's written marketing materials, (b) the failure appeared during the product's stated useful lifespan under normal conditions of use, and (c) the consumer returned the product within the vendor's stated refund window, unless the vendor had, before the sale, clearly disclosed in writing the specific limitation that accounts for the claimed failure. The refund may include reasonable incidental costs but may not exceed the purchase price plus documented incidentals.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aleka bought a $600 portable projector whose marketing materials promised 4K native resolution; the unit displays only at 1080p under any setting. She returned it within the stated 60-day window and had used it normally. Nothing in the vendor's pre-sale disclosures flagged a resolution limitation. She receives a $600 refund plus $35 in documented shipping costs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bersh bought a $400 humidifier whose marketing materials made no claims about quiet operation. He found it too loud and returned it within the refund window. The vendor refuses a refund, reasoning that it made no misleading claim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cimarr bought a $900 treadmill whose marketing materials advertised 300-pound weight capacity, but it failed while he used it at 280 pounds. The stated useful lifespan applies, and he returned it within the window. However, the vendor had included in the pre-sale written disclosures a specific note that the 300-pound figure referred only to static capacity, not dynamic loads. Cimarr demands and receives a full refund.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delka bought a $700 blender whose marketing materials promised commercial-grade performance; it failed during normal use within its stated useful lifespan. She returned it within the refund window with no contrary disclosures applicable. The vendor offers a refund of $2,000 to include lost gig-economy income.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enna bought a $250 coffee grinder that matched its marketing description but broke under normal use fourteen months after the 90-day refund window closed. She demands and receives a full refund.

explanations.correct: Aleka's case satisfies every antecedent condition: the projector failed to deliver the advertised 4K native resolution, the failure appeared within the stated useful lifespan under normal use, and she returned it within the refund window. No pre-sale disclosure flagged a resolution limitation, so the exception does not trigger. The refund equals purchase price plus documented incidentals, matching the proportionality clause.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a). The marketing materials made no claim about quiet operation, so there is no described performance the product failed to meet. The principle does not entitle Bersh to a refund, and the vendor's conclusion is consistent with the principle.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception. The vendor's pre-sale written disclosure specifically addressed the 300-pound figure as a static, not dynamic, rating; that is the limitation accounting for the claimed failure. The principle withholds the refund entitlement.
explanations.D: Violates the proportionality clause. Even though all antecedent conditions are met, the refund may not exceed purchase price plus documented incidentals; lost gig-economy income is neither documented nor an incidental cost of the sort contemplated.
explanations.E: Fails condition (c). The return occurred long after the vendor's stated refund window closed. A different subsidiary principle about long-term durability might be relevant, but the principle stated above does not authorize a refund.

difficultyReason: Three antecedent conditions, an exception turning on the user's own prior consent, and a proportionality clause on remediation. Traps trigger the exception via consent, miss a condition, or exceed the remediation ceiling.
stimulus: A software company is obligated to notify affected users of a data breach only if (a) the breach exposed personal information tied to identifiable individuals, (b) the exposure created a non-trivial risk of harm to those individuals, and (c) the company has a reliable means of contacting the affected users, unless the users had, at account creation, knowingly opted into a public-disclosure research program under which their data was designated for open release. The notification and any remediation offered must be commensurate with the severity of the risk to the affected users.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lumet Software suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information with non-trivial risk of harm. It has reliable contact information, and no user was part of any public-disclosure program. Lumet notifies users and offers a single $5 store credit, disregarding the severity of the risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ivorek Labs suffered a breach exposing anonymized, aggregate usage counts that cannot be tied to any individual. It has reliable contact information for users. Ivorek notifies every user and offers five years of identity-theft insurance to demonstrate its commitment to transparency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juneau Analytics suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information of participants in its public-disclosure research program, all of whom had knowingly opted in at account creation to have their data released openly. Juneau issues no individual notifications, since the users had consented to public release.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Klima Systems suffered a breach exposing identifiable personal information with non-trivial risk of harm, but its contact records were corrupted beyond recovery. It issues a vague public press release. It also announces free identity-theft monitoring priced at a level unrelated to the severity of the risk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helix Software suffered a breach exposing the email addresses and hashed passwords of 80,000 identifiable users, creating a meaningful phishing risk. Helix has verified email addresses for each user, and no user had opted into any public-disclosure research program. Helix notifies all affected users and offers twelve months of credit-monitoring commensurate with the risk.

explanations.correct: Helix's case satisfies every antecedent condition: the breach exposed personal information tied to identifiable users, it created a non-trivial phishing risk, and Helix has reliable email contacts for each user. The exception does not trigger because no user opted into a public-disclosure research program. The notification and twelve months of credit-monitoring are described as commensurate with the risk, satisfying the proportionality clause.
explanations.A: Violates the proportionality clause. A token $5 credit is not commensurate with a non-trivial risk of identity harm. Even though the notification itself was issued, the remediation component fails the principle's proportionality requirement.
explanations.B: Fails condition (a). Anonymized, aggregate usage counts are not tied to identifiable individuals, so the obligation does not attach. The broad remediation also overshoots the proportionality clause.
explanations.C: Triggers the exception, which only negates the obligation to notify. The principle does not affirmatively prescribe the decision to issue no individual notifications at all; it simply withholds the notification obligation. Because the principle does not prescribe the stated judgment, (C) does not conform in the way (E) does.
explanations.D: Fails condition (c). Without reliable means of contacting affected users, the obligation to notify specific users does not attach in the form described, and the unrelated remediation pricing separately violates the proportionality clause.
